entry.evidence: the anomalously high VS values that were observed represented the starting point for the whole work

steps.action: In a preliminary seismic campaign the authors found sites, starting with the top of the San Marco dune, with shallow VS of 400-500 m/s where 100-200 m/s was expected.
steps.quote: During a preliminary seismic campaign, we identified a few sites with anomalously high shear-wave velocity (VS) values already at the surface.

steps.action: Posed the twofold aim: characterize the subsurface of a largely unknown, reclaimed dune system for geologists, and test efficient surface-wave methods in an area with lateral variations.
steps.quote: very little is known about the origin of such a dune system

steps.action: Adopted the Holistic analysis of Surface waves (single 3-component geophone; Z and R group-velocity spectra by Full Velocity Spectrum inversion, RPM curve) and HVSR, jointly inverted by multi-objective Pareto optimization, all developed in the first author's earlier work.
steps.quote: the HS technique requires just one 3-component geophone

steps.action: Checked the sensor premise: low-frequency Guralp and 4.5 Hz Geospace 3-component sensors, used over three years and several seasons, gave the same HVSR curves down to about 0.25 Hz.
steps.quote: have been used providing always consistent results

steps.action: Jointly inverted the Z and R group-velocity spectra (FVS) and the RPM curve at San Marco P1 (top of dune) to a minimum-distance VS profile reaching about 500 m/s at about 3 m depth (Fig. 4, p. 8).
steps.quote: At a depth of about 3 m, VS reaches the considerable value of about 500 m/s

steps.action: Compared the P1 velocities with published VS ranges for uncemented sands (about 150-300 m/s) and concluded that they exceed them.
steps.quote: which cannot be attributed to standard shallow (unconsolidated) [...]

steps.action: Ran a dynamic penetrometer test at P1, which reached refusal on a very hard layer at about 3.7 m, matching the stiff layer in the VS profile (Fig. 5, p. 8).
steps.quote: Penetrometer data appear in excellent agreement with the obtained VS profile

steps.action: Compared raw 3-component active traces and amplitude spectra at P1 and P2 (same source, 50 m offset). P2 signals were slower and more attenuated, and showed water-table P-wave refractions (Fig. 6, p. 9).
steps.quote: terrains at P2 are looser (softer) compared to those at P1

steps.action: Inverted the HS data at P2 (base of dune). The resulting VS profile fits compacted but uncemented sediments; P3 gave a similar profile and is not shown (Fig. 7, p. 10).
steps.quote: typical of good—but not cemented—sedimentary materials

steps.action: Proposed that the high VS reflects a stiff material forming the core of the dune, while the flattened surroundings are ordinary unconsolidated sediments.
steps.quote: represent the properties of the stiff material that constitutes the "core" of the dune itself

steps.action: Designed the Beligna#1 survey from the DTM and surface sand: an ERT section perpendicular to the dune, and HS plus HVSR lines parallel to the dune axis at its centre (HS1) and western edge (HS2).
steps.quote: The ERT section was planned so to be perpendicular to the elongation of the residual dune

steps.action: Jointly inverted the HS group-velocity spectra with HVSR at HS1 and HS2. Results: a stiff (450-500 m/s), resistive sandy centre; a western cover of about 7 m at about 100 m/s, producing a 2.5 Hz HVSR peak with directivity along the dune.
steps.quote: very soft sediments dominate the western part, where the superficial stiff sand-dominated sediments of the residual dune wedge out

steps.action: Checked the profiles against the ERT section and the surface sands, and attributed the 0.43 Hz HVSR peak to deep bedrock by comparison with borehole seismics at Grado.
steps.quote: can be attributed to the deep bedrock—see the borehole seismics performed in the town of Grado

steps.action: Qualified the profiles. The joint-inversion fit is a Pareto compromise, not perfect for each observable, and the deep part rests only on HVSR because of the short offset, so it has limited resolution.
steps.quote: represent just a coarse and average solution (with limited resolution)

steps.action: Recorded a 12-point, 55 m, 3-component passive array along the ERT line to test single-component amplitude spectra and a 2D HVSR section as quick tools for detecting lateral variations.
steps.quote: testing the potentialities of simple procedures based on the spectral analysis of multi-component and multi-offset passive seismic data

steps.action: Compared the 2D HVSR section with the ERT section. The 2.5 Hz peak marks the western edge of the dune, where peat-like soft cover coincides with low resistivity (Fig. 16, p. 16).
steps.quote: the overall consistency of the 2D HVSR section with the ERT data is obvious

steps.action: Excluded a local microtremor source as the cause of the larger western amplitudes: the area is remote and agricultural, and boat transients were removed. The amplification is attributed to stratigraphy.
steps.quote: the larger amplitude in the western part is not related to any local microtremor source

steps.action: Assessed T-component amplitude three ways (raw traces, normalized mean spectra, trace standard deviations) and showed that whole-trace and window-averaged standard deviations agree (Fig. 18, p. 18).
steps.quote: the value of the standard deviation computed considering the whole trace is essentially the same as the value obtained from averaging

steps.action: Derived a processing rule: when amplitudes differ along an array, extract homogeneous trace subsets before computing dispersion. HS arrays were laid along the dune axis to minimize lateral variation.
steps.quote: extract subsets of homogenous traces

steps.action: At the flattened Beligna#2 dune, visible only in drone photos, computed HVSR along a 168 m line, showing a 5.7 Hz peak at 100-120 m and the 0.43 Hz bedrock peak (Fig. 20, p. 19).
steps.quote: the presence of a remarkable HVSR peak at about 5.7 Hz (inline position 100–120 m) is apparent

steps.action: Checked the HVSR transition with T-component spectral ratios and with raw and 5.7 Hz Gaussian-filtered trace standard deviations (340% versus 850% difference), all locating the same abrupt change (Fig. 21, p. 20).
steps.quote: Consistently with the HVSR curves, the comparative analysis of even just the T-component amplitude spectra is useful

steps.action: Again excluded local mechanical or industrial sources as the cause of the amplitude increase at Beligna#2.
steps.quote: the larger amplitude spectra cannot be attributed to any local microtremor source

steps.action: Extracted the homogeneous T-component traces at 100-130 m, computed Love-wave phase dispersion and jointly inverted it with HVSR. The profile shows a 2 m peat cover at 50-90 m/s that explains the 5.7 Hz peak (Fig. 22, p. 21).
steps.quote: The presence of shallow very-soft sediments (peats) in the first couple of meters is responsible for the large HVSR peak

steps.action: Found the Beligna#1 pattern repeated at the independent Beligna#2 dune: a sandy dune bordered on its southern side by a peat channel.
steps.quote: similar to the previous dune (Beligna#1), the sandy dune is bordered by a peat channel

steps.action: Collected surface rock samples, which colleagues identified as bioturbated, medium-grained calcarenite with sparitic cement.
steps.quote: reveal to be medium-grained calcarenite mainly composed of rounded dolomite and limestone intraclasts

steps.action: Linked the cemented relict samples to the high VS along the residual dunes.
steps.quote: observed high VS values along the residual dunes are due to the presence of this kind of materials in the subsurface

steps.action: Took from the dune literature the expectation that wind-dominated settings form longitudinal dunes aligned with the dominant wind.
steps.quote: the formation of longitudinal dunes (with windward slope gentler than the leeward side) is favoured

steps.action: Compared the dominant Bora wind direction (N60E, from published wind data) with the mapped elongation of the paleo-dunes (Fig. 23, p. 22).
steps.quote: This direction is roughly parallel to the elongation of the local paleo-dunes.

steps.action: Rejected the old-coastline origin proposed by earlier studies. Proposed instead an interplay of Isonzo sand supply, Bora wind and lagoonal channels, now seen as peat channels.
steps.quote: the dunes should not be related to an old coastline, as originally proposed by some speculative studies

steps.action: Kept the methodological conclusions: HVSR and simple amplitude-spectra or standard-deviation analysis of passive arrays reveal lateral variations before dispersion analysis, and single-geophone multi-component HS with HVSR gives robust VS profiles.
steps.quote: reveals extremely important to highlight possible lateral variations and should be done prior to the computation of the velocity spectra (dispersion)

No; VS is inferred by joint inversion of surface-wave observables
Characterize subsurface VS and lateral variations, and demonstrate efficient surface-wave tools
Few rivals: local microtremor sources versus stratigraphy for amplitude anomalies; old coastline versus wind-driven longitudinal dunes
Not formally derived; dune-wind alignment is the only discriminating expectation, taken from the literature
Conditions found at three field sites, not set

tree.answer: Yes; the dune-plus-peat-channel pattern recurs at Beligna#1 and Beligna#2
Consistent with penetrometer, ERT, borehole bedrock depth, different sensors and alternative amplitude measures
Kept: methods identify lateral variations; cemented calcarenite dunes bordered by peat channels
No review file supplied; acknowledgements only mention two anonymous reviewers

end.claim: Two kinds of tool are shown, applied in the Grado-Marano perilagoon area, to give reliable VS profiles in a laterally complex area. First, HVSR and simple amplitude-spectra or trace-standard-deviation analysis of multi-offset passive data reveal abrupt lateral variations. Second, single-geophone multi-component HS data jointly inverted with HVSR yield robust VS profiles. The area shows cemented calcarenite residual dunes bordered by low-VS peat channels.

decisive_move.sentence: Checking the passive-array amplitude spectra and filtered trace standard deviations against the HVSR sections (and ERT) at both Beligna sites is what establishes that simple spectral analysis locates lateral variations.

gates.evidence: Action: the P1 anomaly motivated the wider survey and the penetrometer test was run to check the stiff layer (§1.3 ¶2, ¶5); the ERT and HS lines were placed using the DTM and dune axis (§1.4 ¶1), but no stated hypothesis directed acquisition. Claim: the VS profiles could have disagreed with the penetrometer, ERT and borehole bedrock depth. The methodological claim, however, is illustrated rather than scored against a criterion, and the dune-origin interpretation faces only an alignment comparison. Registration: nothing reported fixed in advance.

imports.item: Hilbert transform to compute the Rayleigh-wave particle-motion correlation curve
Multi-objective optimization with Pareto optimality (evolutionary algorithms, Zitzler and Thiele 1999) for joint inversion
Dynamic penetrometer test converted to SPT blow counts
Narrow Gaussian band-pass filter before computing trace standard deviations

novelty_claims.quote: so far very little was known about the local subsurface conditions
but very rarely in near-surface applications
testing a series of efficient and unconventional methodologies based on the analysis of surface waves from both active and passive seismic data

limits: Sub-claims and their statuses: the VS profiles at San Marco and Beligna are estimate_with_resolution, though no uncertainty is given and the deep part is explicitly coarse. The cemented-calcarenite dune core with bordering peat channels is best_explanation. The wind-driven longitudinal origin versus an old coastline is best_explanation, resting on one alignment comparison and cited dune theory. Process gaps: only part of the data is presented, and P3, other conventional methods (SPAC, ESAC, MAAM, MASW) and the further peat-channel data behind Fig. 23 are not shown, so those checks cannot be inspected. No data are available ('Availability of data and materials: None'). The sensor and season comparisons are asserted, with a technical report only promised. No inversion uncertainty or Pareto-front spread is reported; the minimum-distance model is shown alone. The methods are the first author's own and are not compared quantitatively here against MASW or SPAC on the same data. The rock lithology comes from colleagues by personal communication. Inference: the paper reads as a field demonstration and regional characterization, not a test of a stated hypothesis. Hence composition none_fits: it mixes an anomaly-driven entry, inherited capability and found-condition site repetition (partly trace_series) without rivals until the final geological discussion. No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded.

disagreements.target: Marocco 1991; Lenardon and Marocco 1994 (dunes as an ancient shoreline)
disagreements.support: Dune elongation roughly parallel to the dominant Bora wind, plus cited longitudinal-dune theory and the identified lagoonal peat channels; no direct dating or facies test.
disagreements.quote: the dunes should not be related to an old coastline, as originally proposed by some speculative studies

disagreements.support: Argued from the non-uniqueness of single-observable inversion and the authors' earlier comparative studies; no side-by-side comparison on these data is shown.
disagreements.quote: free from the ambiguities that characterize the standard MASW/SPAC/ESAC/MAAM methodologies based on the analysis of just one component

disagreements.target: Use of HVSR to estimate site effects in seismic hazard studies
disagreements.support: Cites Seekins et al. 1996 and Perron et al. 2018; no new evidence offered here.
disagreements.quote: its significance in estimating site effects in seismic hazard studies is highly questionable

disagreements.target: Common simplification that Rayleigh-wave particle motion is retrograde
disagreements.support: Cited earlier RPM work, and P2 data where the observed particle motion is largely prograde (Fig. 7).
disagreements.quote: despite the simplification often made, the particle motion induced by Rayleigh waves is usually far from being retrograde

disagreements.target: Soil classification from large-scale geological or sedimentological maps
disagreements.support: VS changes dramatically over a few meters at Beligna, which such maps cannot resolve.
disagreements.quote: strongly discourage any attempt to classify the soil on the basis of large-scale geological or sedimentological maps

alternatives_considered.reason: Group velocities can be defined with a single geophone; multi-component data reduce ambiguity

alternatives_considered.chosen: HS and HVSR emphasized in the paper
alternatives_considered.alternatives: SPAC, ESAC, multi-component MASW, MAAM (also applied but not presented)
alternatives_considered.reason: Simple field procedures and light equipment

alternatives_considered.chosen: Full Velocity Spectrum inversion of the whole frequency-velocity matrix
alternatives_considered.reason: FVS is intrinsically multimodal and avoids modal interpretation

alternatives_considered.chosen: Joint multi-objective inversion of several observables, reporting the minimum-distance model
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Inversion of a single observable (nearly perfect misfit); other models on the Pareto front
alternatives_considered.reason: Single observables give non-unique solutions; the minimum-distance model is the best compromise

alternatives_considered.chosen: HVSR frequency range kept lower than that of the velocity spectra in joint inversion
alternatives_considered.reason: HVSR is particularly relevant in the low-frequency range

alternatives_considered.chosen: Guralp CMG-40T and Geospace 4.5 Hz 3-component sensors used interchangeably for HVSR
alternatives_considered.reason: Only an identical response of the three components matters for a spectral ratio
P3 VS profile very similar to P2; brevity

alternatives_considered.reason: Minimal lateral variations expected along the elongation, confirmed by HVSR

alternatives_considered.chosen: Dispersion computed on homogeneous trace subsets
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Dispersion from the entire 12-channel (or 168 m) array
alternatives_considered.reason: Whole-array velocity spectra would be extremely complex, possibly unintelligible, not reducible to 1D

alternatives_considered.chosen: Whole-trace standard deviation after transient removal
alternatives_considered.reason: Transients removed, so the two coincide

alternatives_considered.chosen: Standard deviations of 5.7 Hz Gaussian-filtered traces
alternatives_considered.reason: Filtering isolates the amplitude difference at the HVSR peak frequency

alternatives_considered.chosen: Love-wave (T-component) dispersion jointly inverted with HVSR at Beligna#2
alternatives_considered.reason: Love waves usually provide clearer information
